commentary:
The Strait of Hormuz standoff is again the market's organizing principle this morning. Tehran refused to soften its conditions for reopening the waterway after Trump rejected its latest proposal, and crude ripped higher — Brent up 3.6% through $108, WTI near $96, heating oil +4.3% with the prompt Brent spread at its firmest backwardation since April. Saudi Arabia's repaired East-West pipeline resuming exports offered only marginal offset. The knock-on is a classic supply-shock risk tone: Treasuries fell across the curve with the 10-year yield through 5.2%, US equity futures dropped (Nasdaq -0.8%) as oil rekindled inflation worries, and the dollar sits near a two-month high on firming Fed rate-hike bets after last week's first hike in three years.

Note what didn't work: gold fell 3.2% and silver nearly 5% despite the geopolitics — with the Fed back in tightening mode and real yields grinding higher, the precious complex is trading as a rates-and-dollar casualty, not a haven. Copper's 1.9% slide adds a growth-worry signal even as China's cabinet pledged stronger policy support to hit its target. Ags were the other sore spot — soybeans -1.8%, corn and wheat down over 1% — after the Trump-Xi summit's tariff-cut lists conspicuously excluded soybeans and LNG, leaving the trade complex wanting more.

Transmission is straightforward: energy strength feeds sticky inflation, which pressures the long end (heavy issuance and the AI financing wave are already keeping term premia elevated), which caps index futures and supports the dollar.
